title: The sand mandala
hookLine: monks build a mandala of colored sand for days, then sweep it into a river

lines: A LOW TABLE, A FEW MONKS.
SAND, A FEW GRAINS AT A TIME.
cards: A museum lobby, or a college gym. A few Tibetan monks lean over a low table. For days, sometimes weeks, they tap thin metal funnels, and colored sand trickles out a few grains at a time.

People come back every afternoon to watch it grow: palaces, gates, lotus petals, lines finer than a pencil could draw. Then, on the last day, with everyone watching, a monk draws a line straight through the middle.

teach.h: MANDALA — CIRCLE, A MAP OF AWAKENING.

teach.b: In Tibetan practice it's more than a pattern: it's a map of an awakened world, often the palace of a Buddha or deity seen from above, with four gates facing the four directions, bright walls, and the deity at the very center.
People meditate on it, and some rituals are performed around it. Mandalas can be painted, built in three dimensions, or pictured in the mind. The sand mandala is made to be fragile.

teach.h: SAND, GRAIN BY GRAIN, FOR DAYS.
teach.b: The monks' narrow metal funnel has ridges along its side; rub a rod across them and it vibrates, and the sand falls grain by grain.
Teams work from the center outward, following exact measurements handed down in the texts. Then comes the ending, the part people remember.
When the rituals are complete, the lines are cut through and the sand is swept toward the center into one gray-brown pile. Some is given to the people watching, as a blessing.
The rest is carried to a river or stream and poured in, so the blessing flows out into the world, like the wind through the prayer flags. Why build something so beautiful and then destroy it?
Tibetan teachers give more than one reason. The sweeping teaches impermanence, which you've met since the first sight of an old man. It teaches letting go of what we make.
And it shows the blessing was never meant to stay in one room. The work was real. The beauty was real.

how: Tibetan monks construct sand mandalas for particular rituals and, increasingly, for public events; when the ceremony ends they dismantle the mandala, give some sand to those present and pour the rest into flowing water.

a sacred circle that maps an awakened world

games.q: the monks have spent two weeks on the sand mandala. it's perfect. the rituals are done. what happens next?
o: glue it down and hang it in the museum.
cut through it, sweep it up and pour it in a river.
cover it and save it for next year.
games.why: it's swept to the center; some sand is given away and the rest goes into flowing water, a teaching on impermanence and letting go.

practice: Arrange a few things near you into a small pattern, coins, pens, leaves, and take care with it for a moment. Then gently mix it up and let it go, noticing any small tug of not wanting to.
Sit, and let each breath arrive and pass, built and swept away.

wordCard.voice: Mandala. A circle: a map of an awakened world, built in sand with great care, then swept away and poured into the river.

orig.note: Sanskrit maṇḍala: circle. Tibetan: kyilkhor, 'center and surround'.

carryVoice: Your line: swept away. The work was careful, and the letting go was part of it. Day three hundred fourteen, done.

sources.ref: Tibetan ritual practice of the sand mandala (e.g. the Kalachakra mandala)
